disease_name.evidence: Field Identification of Citrus Blight

affected_parts.evidence: begin to wilt and to exhibit leaf loss, reduced growth flushes, die back and general decline... As the xylem vessels in the trunk become plugged with amorphous occlusions, water transport is reduced, causing a general wilt appearance.

summary.value: Affected trees wilt and exhibit leaf loss, reduced growth flushes, dieback and general decline, often beginning in one sector before expanding to the entire tree; vegetative sprouts may develop on the trunk or interior branches and zinc-deficiency patterns develop in the leaves.
summary.evidence: begin to wilt and to exhibit leaf loss, reduced growth flushes, die back and general decline (Figure 1). In early stages of blight, the symptoms may be restricted to one sector of the tree and then expand to the entire tree... vegetative sprouts may be produced on the trunk or on larger interior branches near the trunk... zinc accumulates in the bark and outer xylem tissue, and zinc deficiency patterns develop in the leaves.

diagnostic_features.value: Blighted trees fail to accept water injected into the trunk via a syringe test (less than 0.5 ml in 10 seconds for fully blighted trees vs. at least 3 ml in 10 seconds for healthy trees), whereas trees declining from other diseases or disorders will accept water readily.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Healthy trees with no visual symptoms in the canopy should accept at least 3 ml in 10 seconds, whereas fully blighted trees will accept less than 0.5 ml of water in the same 10 second period... Trees infected with blight will accept very little or no water, whereas a tree declining from other diseases or disorders will accept water readily, thus providing an easy field diagnostic test for citrus blight.

extractions.source_title: PP-180/CG038: 2025–2026 Florida Citrus Production Guide: Blight

disease_name.evidence: Citrus blight is a wilt-and-decline disease of citrus, and its cause has not been determined.

affected_parts.evidence: mild wilting and grayish cast to the foliage ... extensive twig dieback ... presence of amorphous plugs in the xylem ... presence of blight-associated citrus proteins in roots and leaves

summary.value: Mild wilting and a grayish cast to the foliage, often with zinc deficiency symptoms, followed by rapid decline with extensive twig dieback, off-season flowering, and small fruit.
summary.evidence: The first symptoms on huanglongbing (HLB)-free trees are usually a mild wilting and grayish cast to the foliage, often accompanied by zinc deficiency symptoms on trees. Trees rapidly decline with extensive twig dieback, off-season flowering, and small fruit.

diagnostic_features.value: High zinc content in trunk bark and wood; amorphous plugs in the xylem; failure to absorb water injected into the trunk (trees take up no water regardless of pressure applied); and presence of blight-associated citrus proteins in roots and leaves.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Citrus blight is characterized by (1) high zinc content in trunk bark and wood; (2) presence of amorphous plugs in the xylem; (3) failure to absorb water injected into the trunk; and (4) presence of blight-associated citrus proteins in roots and leaves.

look_alikes.evidence: Blight symptoms can be confused with other decline diseases (e.g., HLB, tristeza decline, etc.) ... Healthy trees or trees declining from phytophthora root rot, nematodes, water damage, tristeza, or HLB will usually take up about 10 ml of water in 30 seconds.

extractions.source_title: Alternative Management Approaches of Citrus Diseases Caused by Penicillium digitatum (Green Mold) and Penicillium italicum (Blue Mold)

disease_name.evidence: Green mold ( Penicillium digitatum ) and blue mold ( Penicillium italicum ) are among the most economically impactful post-harvest diseases of citrus fruit worldwide.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Green mold, caused by Penicillium digitatum Sacc, and blue mold, caused by Penicillium italicum Wehmer, result in substantial economic losses around the globe

type_of_disease.evidence: P. digitatum , a necrotrophic fungus infecting citrus species via mechanical wounds and environmental factors such as cold, wind, insects, and hail, accounts for ~90% of total post-harvest losses alone

summary.value: The infected fruit produces white mycelia and greenish conidia; the mycelium breaks down fruit cell walls causing shrinkage into a sunken mummified form, and infected pericarp and mesocarp cells plasmolyze, causing a soft watery spot and rotting the fruit.
summary.evidence: The infected fruit then produces white mycelia and greenish conidia, a characteristic symptoms of green mold (Lin et al., 2019 ). The mycelium produces enzymes that break down fruit cell walls and initiate shrinkage, resulting in a sunken mummified form (Papoutsis et al., 2019 ). The infected pericarp and mesocarp cells plasmolyze, causing a soft watery spot, and the fruit is rotted

diagnostic_features.value: A thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by decaying peel surrounds green mold spores, distinguishing it from blue mold.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Although initial lesions caused by green mold resemble blue mold disease, a thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by decaying peel surrounds green mold spores

disease_name.evidence: Green mold ( Penicillium digitatum ) and blue mold ( Penicillium italicum ) are among the most economically impactful post-harvest diseases of citrus fruit worldwide.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: blue mold, caused by Penicillium italicum Wehmer, result in substantial economic losses around the globe

type_of_disease.evidence: The P. digitatum and P. italicum fungi have a short disease cycle ranging from 3 to 5 days at 25°C and reproduce one to two billion conidial spores

summary.value: Spores of P. italicum are encapsulated in narrow white mycelium bounded by fluffy, water-soaked rind; the white mycelium grows into infected tissue and sporulates blue conidia.
summary.evidence: Spores of P. italicum are encapsulated in narrow white mycelium bounded by fluffy, water-soaked rind (Holmes and Eckert, 1999 ; Palou et al., 2002a , b , 2008 ; Talibi et al., 2014 ; Papoutsis et al., 2019 ). The white mycelium grows and digs into the infected tissue, sporulating blue conidia

diagnostic_features.value: Narrow white mycelium bounded by fluffy, water-soaked rind with blue sporulating conidia; a nesting-type pathogen that spreads rapidly in packed containers to infect adjacent fruits.
diagnostic_features.evidence: P. italicum is a nesting-type pathogen that spreads rapidly in packed containers to infect adjacent fruits (Ladaniya, 2008 ) even at lower temperatures in cold storage

affected_parts.evidence: The disease affects all parts of the tree canopy -  leaves, twigs and fruit As the disease progresses, it will cause the whole tree to decline

summary.value: Early symptoms are vein yellowing and an asymmetrical chlorosis (blotchy mottle) on leaves; affected trees show twig dieback, yellow shoots, and stunting. Fruit are often small, lopsided, fail to color properly (remain green at the stylar end), may have a curved central core, aborted seeds, and a salty bitter taste.
summary.evidence: The early symptoms of HLB on leaves are vein yellowing and an asymmetrical chlorosis referred to as “blotchy mottle.”

diagnostic_features.value: Blotchy mottle — an asymmetrical random pattern of yellowing (chlorosis) on leaves that is not the same on the right and left sides of the leaf — is the most diagnostic symptom, especially on sweet orange. A yellow stain may be present just beneath the peduncle (stem) on a cut fruit, and fruit often remain green at the stylar end with a curved central core.
diagnostic_features.evidence: The blotchy mottle symptom is the most diagnostic symptom of the disease, especially on sweet orange.

look_alikes.evidence: The blotchy mottle symptom also may be confused with other diseases or damage such as severe forms of  citrus tristeza virus (CTV) , Phytophthora root rot, water logging,  citrus blight , leafminer tunnels or stubborn, a disease that is not known to be present in Florida.
